DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this research is the first clinical
trial on the effectiveness of SO in the management of acute der-
matitis caused by radiation in patients with BC. Owing to the lack
of similar studies in this field, there is no basis for the details of
the findings. Radiotherapy plays a vital role in the BC management
of patients. Most BC patients who receive chest wall radiotherapy
experience ARD during the course of radiation therapy or shortly
after its completion. Acute dermatitis from chest wall radiotherapy
can reduce radiotherapy tolerance, negatively affect the quality of
life, disrupt treatment, and be challenging.
Radiation dermatitis is a
side effect of BC radiotherapy. Radiation damages keratinocytes, caus-
ing oxidative stress due to the generation of reactive oxygen species
linked to tissue destruction.

show, in the second and third weeks, no significant difference was
observed between the two groups in terms of dermatitis (p < 0.05).
In the fourth week, in the case group, dermatitis grade 0 was 35%,
grade 1 was 65%, and grade 2 was 0% , while in the control group, they
were 10%, 75%, and 15%, respectively, showing this difference to be
statistically significant (p = 0.046).
Also, in the fifth week, in the case group, dermatitis grade 0 was
25%, grade 1 was 70%, and grade 2 was 5%, while in the control group,
they were 0%, 80%, and 20%, respectively; this difference was statis-
tically significant (p = 0.032). According to the fitting GEE results, the
odds ratio (OR) of the control group for high-grade dermatitis was more
than two times of the case group, which was significant (p = 0.047;
OR = 2.09). This result also demonstrated that the cases of dermati-
tis increased with time passage during the course of radiotherapy. Age
was not significant in increasing dermatitis (p = 0.617; OR = 2.09).
We observed no allergic or any adverse reaction to SO in the control
group (Chart 1).
